client.name: Wafra Agro Group
client.profile: Prospective client, courted from a competitor. Glossy presentation, audited financials, impatient for a quick answer. The ratios look clean — almost too clean.

request: "We're consolidating our banking. KD 2,000,000 STRL to start, and there's much more business behind it if you move fast. Our audited numbers are excellent — your competitor pre-approved us last week."

ratios.label: Current ratio
ratios.hint: Healthy on its face.

ratios.label: Receivable days
ratios.hint: Receivables nearly doubled in a year while sales grew 8%. Something is sitting in that line.

ratios.label: Notes to accounts, note 14
ratios.value: KD 1,040,000 of receivables due from 'Wafra International Trading WLL' — a related party, invoiced 28–31 December
ratios.hint: 40% of receivables are to a sister company, booked in the last four days of the financial year.

decisions.prompt: You've read the pack, including the notes. What's your honest read?

options.label: Probable window dressing: year-end sales to a related party inflate revenue and receivables — the 'clean' ratios may be decorated
options.feedback: That's the pattern: invoice a sister company in the last week of December, book it as sales, and the year ends prettier than it was. The audit can be technically clean while the picture misleads.

options.label: Strong group with healthy intercompany trade — normal for agro conglomerates
options.feedback: Intercompany trade is normal; KD 1M of it materialising in the final four days of the financial year is not. Timing plus counterparty plus size = the window-dressing signature.

options.label: The auditors signed it, so the numbers are reliable as presented
options.feedback: An unqualified audit means the statements follow the standards — not that the December related-party sales reflect commercial reality. Credit reads behind the opinion.

options.label: Receivables growth simply reflects the sales growth
options.feedback: Sales grew 8%; receivables grew 86%. The arithmetic of that explanation fails before the related-party note even enters the room.

decisions.prompt: Khaled wants an answer this week. Your move?

options.label: Request the receivables aging, the related-party sales contracts, and post-year-end collection evidence before any approval
options.feedback: The one test window dressing can't pass: show me the cash. If the December receivables collected in January, fine. If they're still sitting there — you have your answer.

options.label: Approve KD 2,000,000 — audited numbers, competitor pre-approval, move fast
options.feedback: You lent KD 2M against ratios that note 14 had already undressed. 'Your competitor approved it' is the oldest pressure tactic in banking precisely because it works.

options.label: Approve KD 1,000,000 now to win the relationship, verify later
options.feedback: Half the money against the same unanswered question. 'Lend first, verify later' is not a sequence credit recognises.

options.label: Decline outright — too suspicious to touch
options.feedback: Defensible — discipline beats deal-hunger. But a request for collection evidence costs nothing and would tell you whether you just declined a dressed-up balance sheet or a genuinely good client.

decisions.prompt: Khaled responds: "The aging is internal. The related-party contracts are confidential. Take the audited numbers or we go elsewhere." Final answer?

options.label: Decline politely — a client who won't show collection evidence on KD 1M of related-party receivables has answered the question
options.feedback: Refusing routine transparency on the exact item in doubt is itself the finding. The deals you decline are part of your track record too — let the competitor have this one.

options.label: Approve anyway — competitive markets demand flexibility
options.feedback: You waived the only verification that mattered, under deadline pressure, for a prospect. This is precisely how banks meet their worst clients.

options.label: Approve with a personal guarantee from Khaled as comfort
options.feedback: A PG from the CFO of a group that may be dressing its numbers is comfort made of the same material as the numbers.

options.label: Offer KD 500,000 'starter facility' to keep the door open
options.feedback: A quarter of the money against zero of the transparency. Small bad loans are still bad loans — and they grow.

learn: Window dressing signature: year-end related-party sales inflating receivables and ratios. The unbeatable test is post-year-end collection evidence — and a client who refuses to show it has shown you everything.

client.name: Marina Heights Real Estate Co.
client.profile: Established developer, two completed mid-rise projects. Now proposing their most ambitious tower yet — and their most leveraged.

request: "An 18-million-dinar residential tower near the waterfront. We want the bank in for KD 14,400,000 — 80% of cost — released up front so we can move fast. Presales will catch up; they always do."

ratios.label: Loan-to-cost requested
ratios.hint: At 80% the developer has KD 3.6M at risk in an 18M project — the bank carries the project; the developer carries an option.

ratios.label: Presales coverage
ratios.hint: 70% of units face market risk 30 months out. Presales are the project's real repayment source.

ratios.label: DSCR / exit
ratios.hint: No rental income, no corporate cash flow behind it — sales or nothing.

decisions.prompt: 80% LTC, upfront release, 30% presold. What does the bank offer?

options.label: Project Finance KD 9,000,000 (50% LTC) — milestone drawdowns against certified construction progress, equity in first
options.feedback: The shape of survivable development finance: the developer's money builds the foundations, the bank's money follows verified progress, and at 50% LTC there's cushion if the market turns mid-build.

options.label: KD 14,400,000 upfront — speed is a competitive advantage
options.feedback: Eighty percent of an 18M project wired on day one, secured by a hole in the ground and 30% presales. If anything slips — costs, sales, the market — the bank owns the problem at full size.

options.label: KD 14,400,000 but milestone-released
options.feedback: Milestones fix the disbursement risk, not the leverage: at 80% LTC the developer can walk away from trouble far more cheaply than the bank can. Structure controls timing; only equity controls commitment.

options.label: Decline — 30% presales is too thin for a project this size
options.feedback: A defensible credit stance — plenty of committees would agree. But a 50% LTC milestone structure with presale covenants makes this bankable; declining forfeits a strong client the structure could have protected.

decisions.prompt: Security package for the tower financing?

options.label: First mortgage over land & development + assignment of all presale proceeds into a project account + corporate guarantee
options.feedback: The trinity of development finance: the asset, the cash flow, and the sponsor — with buyer payments flowing into an account the bank controls, not the developer's general coffers.

options.label: First mortgage over the land only
options.feedback: Necessary but not sufficient: half-built towers sell terribly. The presale proceeds are the living cash of this deal — capture them.

options.label: Assignment of presale proceeds only — the mortgage slows things down
options.feedback: If sales stall, the proceeds assignment is an assignment of nothing — and the bank holds no claim on the only hard asset.

options.label: Chairman's personal guarantee — he's good for it
options.feedback: A PG against a KD 9M project exposure is a comfort letter with a signature. The project itself must collateralise the project.

decisions.prompt: One covenant matters more than the rest. Which do you insist on?

options.label: Minimum presales threshold before each drawdown tranche (e.g. 50% sold before the second tranche releases)
options.feedback: It ties the bank's escalating exposure to proven market demand — the project must keep earning its financing as it rises. If sales stall, drawdowns stall, and the loss stops growing.

options.label: Cost overruns funded by the developer before further drawdowns
options.feedback: A genuinely important covenant — overruns are how 50% LTC quietly becomes 70%. Second only to the presales trigger, which protects against the bigger risk: building something nobody's buying.

options.label: Monthly site progress reports to the bank
options.feedback: Reports inform; they don't protect. Knowing the tower is on schedule says nothing about whether anyone is buying the units.

options.label: No additional covenants — the mortgage is protection enough
options.feedback: The mortgage protects against total loss, badly and slowly. Covenants prevent the situations where you'd need it.

facilitySummary: Project Finance KD 9.0M (50% LTC, milestone drawdowns)

plantedError.prompt: First drawdown request arrives. Legal review flags the security file. What's wrong?

options.label: The mortgage over the land is signed but not yet registered with the authorities
options.feedback: Correct — an unregistered mortgage is legally unperfected; another creditor could register ahead of the bank. No drawdown until registration is complete. Security perfection precedes utilisation, always.

options.label: The mortgage deed should name the contractor, not the developer
options.feedback: The developer owns the land — the mortgage is correctly granted by them.

options.label: Nothing — signed documents are sufficient to release funds
options.feedback: Signed but unregistered means unperfected. Registration is what makes the mortgage real against third parties.

learn: Development finance survives on three disciplines: real developer equity in first (≈50% LTC), drawdowns chasing verified progress, and a presales covenant that halts the bank's exposure the moment the market stops buying.

client.name: Al Tijaria Electronics Co.
client.profile: Annual review time. Eight-year client, decent payer, friendly relationship. The facility file, however, has developed a smell.

request: "Renewal should be a formality, right? The STRL works perfectly for us — honestly it's the backbone of the company now. Same terms as always, KD 1,500,000."

figures.label: Drawdown rollovers
figures.value: Every 90-day drawdown rolled at maturity, repaid by redrawing

figures.label: New on balance sheet
figures.value: Warehouse property, KD 950,000, acquired 13 months ago

ratios.label: STRL behaviour
ratios.hint: A revolving loan that hasn't revolved in 14 months isn't revolving — it's a frozen block of debt being refinanced every 90 days.

ratios.label: Timing
ratios.value: Hardcore utilisation began the month the warehouse was bought
ratios.hint: Follow the dates: the 'working capital' line stopped revolving exactly when KD 950,000 of property appeared.

ratios.label: True working capital need (recomputed)
ratios.hint: Pre-computed from current inventory and receivable levels — less than half the limit.

decisions.prompt: Diagnose the file before you touch the renewal.

options.label: The STRL was diverted to buy the warehouse — short-term money is trapped in a long-term asset, rolled every 90 days to hide the mismatch
options.feedback: The dates don't lie: hardcore utilisation began with the property purchase. Each rollover papers over a structural problem — working capital money doing a term loan's job.

options.label: The business simply grew into the limit — renew and move on
options.feedback: Growth shows up in sales and inventory; the recomputed need is KD 600,000 against a KD 1.5M frozen balance. The other KD 900,000 is wearing a warehouse.

options.label: Normal seasonal hardcore — most STRLs look like this sometimes
options.feedback: Sometimes, briefly, yes. Fourteen consecutive months synchronised with a property purchase is not a season — it's a structure failure with a calendar attached.

options.label: Suspicious activity — freeze the account and escalate to compliance
options.feedback: Buying a warehouse with mispurposed working capital is bad structure, not money laundering. The remedy is restructuring, not a compliance freeze that torches an 8-year relationship.

decisions.prompt: Now the renewal decision. What do you propose?

options.label: Carve out KD 900,000 into a 7-year term loan secured by warehouse mortgage; renew the STRL at KD 600,000 — its true cycle size
options.feedback: Each dinar back in its right instrument: the property financed by a term loan that amortises from operating cash flow, and a working capital line that can finally revolve again. The honest fix.

options.label: Renew as is — it's rolling fine, why disturb a paying client
options.feedback: You renewed a disguised term loan with no amortisation, no matching security, wrong pricing. 'Rolling fine' is what every evergreen looks like until the quarter it doesn't.

options.label: Demand the KD 900,000 excess be repaid within 60 days
options.feedback: The money is in the building — he can't repay it in 60 days without selling the warehouse or finding another bank in a hurry. An impossible demand is not de-risking.

options.label: Convert the entire KD 1,500,000 to a term loan
options.feedback: It fixes the mismatch but overshoots: KD 600,000 of genuine revolving need is now locked in amortising debt, and he'll be back for a new working capital line within a quarter. The carve-out is more precise.

decisions.prompt: Security for the restructured package?

options.label: First mortgage over the warehouse for the term loan + PG; STRL secured as before
options.feedback: The asset that caused the problem now secures its own financing — registered, proportionate, and the structure self-documents what went wrong and how it was fixed.

options.label: PG only — the relationship carries it
options.feedback: A KD 900,000 term carve-out with an unencumbered warehouse sitting in plain view, and you took a signature instead. The committee will ask why; there is no good answer.

options.label: Keep existing security unchanged across the new structure
options.feedback: The existing security was sized for a revolving trade line, not a 7-year property loan. New structure, new security analysis.

options.label: Mortgage over the warehouse + assignment of all receivables + PG + 25% cash margin
options.feedback: Nothing wrong with any element — but stacking maximum security on a cooperative 8-year client who's accepting your restructure reads as punitive. Proportion is also a credit skill.

learn: A revolving facility that never revolves is the loudest red flag in portfolio monitoring. Trace where the money went, then rebuild: term assets into term loans with matching security, and the STRL back to its true cycle size.

client.name: Najmat Catering Services
client.profile: Quality operator, client for 5 years. Just won the contract of their life — which is precisely what worries you.

request: "We won the national airline's catering contract — five years, KD 4,000,000 a year! We need a KD 400,000 performance bond, a KD 600,000 advance guarantee, and about KD 1,200,000 for the new flight kitchen. This contract changes everything."

ratios.label: DSCR on the kitchen TL (7 yrs, incl. contract)
ratios.hint: Comfortable — as long as the airline contract is alive.

ratios.label: DSCR excluding the airline contract
ratios.hint: The uncomfortable twin: without this one customer, the kitchen loan doesn't service. The contract isn't an upside — it's the whole deal.

ratios.label: Customer concentration
ratios.hint: One termination clause away from a different company.

decisions.prompt: Before structuring — name the dominant risk in this file.

options.label: Customer concentration: at 85% of revenue, the airline relationship IS the company — and the financed kitchen is single-purpose
options.feedback: Exactly. The 1.6x DSCR is a derivative of one contract's survival. Everything in the structure must answer: what happens to the bank if the airline walks in year three?

options.label: Execution risk — can they actually scale to airline volumes?
options.feedback: Real and worth covenanting — but a capable 5-year operator scaling a known business is a manageable risk. The 85% concentration is the one that can't be managed, only structured around.

options.label: No major risk — a 5-year contract with the national airline is as good as government paper
options.feedback: Airline contracts carry termination clauses, service-level conditions and renegotiation rights. Treating one customer at 85% as risk-free is how concentration losses are born.

options.label: Interest rate risk on the 7-year term loan
options.feedback: A footnote risk in a file whose headline is a single customer holding 85% of the revenue.

decisions.prompt: Structure the package for a deal that is one contract deep.

options.label: Full package — PB + APG + TL/7yrs — with assignment of airline contract proceeds, advance via the bank, and an early-amortisation trigger if the contract is lost
options.feedback: You financed the opportunity and structured the concentration: contract cash flows through the bank, and if the airline ever exits, the loan starts repaying immediately instead of discovering the 0.6x DSCR the hard way.

options.label: The LGs only — decline the kitchen loan until revenue diversifies
options.feedback: The contract requires the kitchen; without the capex there is no contract to win bonds for. This declines the deal while pretending not to.

options.label: Full package, clean and simple — a strong contract needs no scaffolding
options.feedback: KD 2.2M of exposure resting unsecured on one customer relationship. The contract is the repayment source; it cannot also be the security by just existing.

options.label: Decline — 85% concentration is outside any sane appetite
options.feedback: Concentration is a structuring problem before it's a declining problem. With assigned proceeds and an exit trigger, this is a bankable deal a competitor will happily structure properly.

decisions.prompt: Complete the security and covenant package.

options.label: Assignment of contract proceeds + lien over kitchen equipment + PG + DSCR covenant tested quarterly
options.feedback: Cash flow captured, asset charged, owner committed, and a quarterly tripwire that surfaces deterioration while it's still a conversation rather than a workout.

options.label: Assignment of contract proceeds only
options.feedback: The single most important piece — but a single-purpose flight kitchen with no lien and no covenant leaves recovery thin if the one customer leaves.

options.label: Mortgage over the CEO's personal villa
options.feedback: Punitive optics, painful realisation, and it sidesteps the deal's own assets and cash flows — which are sitting there, assignable.

options.label: 20% cash margin on the LGs and nothing on the term loan
options.feedback: Margins the small, contingent exposures and leaves the KD 1.2M cash loan naked — security allocated upside down.

learn: Concentration isn't declined — it's structured: assign the contract proceeds, charge the financed asset, and build an early-amortisation trigger so the loan exits when the contract does. Always read the DSCR both with and without the star customer.

client.name: Al-Dhow Marine Services
client.profile: Your old discounting client — two rough years later. Lost the port authority renewal to a competitor, two years of losses, OD maxed for months. Today he looks tired, and he's brought a proposal.

request: "I need KD 500,000, short-term. I'll be straight with you — most of it repays what I owe Gulf Premier Bank; they're squeezing me. Clear them, and I can focus on winning the port contract back next quarter. You know me, you know I'm good for it."

ratios.label: Purpose of new money
ratios.hint: Not one fil funds operations or recovery — it relocates an existing default from their books to ours.

ratios.label: Repayment source
ratios.value: A contract not yet re-tendered, not yet won
ratios.hint: Hope, with a date attached. And the date moves.

ratios.label: Current exposure status
ratios.value: OD hardcore 7 months, interest serviced erratically
ratios.hint: By conduct, this account is already migrating toward watchlist on its own.

decisions.prompt: Name what's actually being proposed here.

options.label: Evergreening by transfer: new money to repay another lender, dressed as a bridge to a contract that doesn't exist yet
options.feedback: Precisely. Gulf Premier is escaping, and the proposal nominates us to fund their exit. New money that creates no new capacity to repay is a bigger loss on a delay timer.

options.label: A reasonable consolidation — one banking relationship is easier to manage
options.feedback: Consolidation is for performing debt. Consolidating a defaulted exposure out of a competitor's book into ours, secured by hope, has a different name — and the other bank is sending flowers.

options.label: A liquidity bridge to the port contract re-award
options.feedback: A bridge needs a far bank: the re-tender is unconfirmed, the win is hypothetical, and his track record on the last round is that he lost it. This bridge lands in water.

options.label: Fraud — report him and exit entirely
options.feedback: Bader was honest about the purpose — that's distress, not deception. The discipline is refusing bad structure while managing the genuine workout we already own.

decisions.prompt: What do you actually do with this relationship?

options.label: No new money. Restructure OUR exposure: term-out the KD 280,000 hardcore OD over a realistic tenor, tighten security, and set a monitoring plan
options.feedback: The professional workout: you can't fix his Gulf Premier problem, but you can stop ours from growing and give the genuine debt a repayment shape his real cash flow can carry.

options.label: Lend the KD 500,000 — five years of relationship deserves the benefit of the doubt
options.feedback: Exposure grows from 280K to 780K, repayment source unchanged: a contract nobody has tendered. The relationship argument just doubled the loss it was invoked to prevent.

options.label: Lend KD 250,000 — half measures, shared pain
options.feedback: Half of a loan with no repayment source is half a write-off, plus the original. There is no right size for new money here.

options.label: Call the OD and start legal recovery immediately
options.feedback: Against a cooperative, honest client with real (if struggling) operations, immediate legal action collapses any recovery value and guarantees the worst outcome for both sides. Workout first; war later, if ever.

decisions.prompt: Internally — how must this account now be treated?

options.label: Reclassify to watchlist, provision per policy, quarterly review with a documented action plan
options.feedback: The classification reflects what the account already is. Honest grading hurts the quarter and saves the year — and the documented plan is what turns a watchlist entry into a recovery story.

options.label: Keep it performing — the restructure technically cures the arrears
options.feedback: Restructuring to dodge classification is the accounting arm of evergreening. The auditors and the regulator both know this move — and it has their least favourite name.

options.label: Straight to legal/recovery classification
options.feedback: Premature — a cooperative client in an agreed restructure with live operations is a watchlist case. Over-classifying forecloses the workout you just designed.

options.label: Defer the decision until next annual review
options.feedback: Classification follows facts, and the facts are nine months old already. Deferral isn't caution; it's the file lying to the committee for another year.

plantedError.prompt: Preparing the restructure memo, you check the file's supporting documents. What's the gap?

options.label: The latest financials on file are 18 months old — the restructure would be approved on stale numbers
options.feedback: Correct. A workout decision needs current numbers — interim accounts, recent bank statements, an updated order book. Restructuring on 18-month-old financials is navigation by an old map.

options.label: The original facility agreement is missing the bank's logo
options.feedback: Cosmetic. The binding content is signatures and terms, not letterhead.

options.label: Nothing — the file supports the decision
options.feedback: Check the dates on the financials: 18 months stale. No restructure should be approved against numbers that old.

learn: New money that repays another lender is evergreening by transfer — it adds loss, not capacity. The workout discipline: no new money, restructure what you own against real cash flow, classify honestly, monitor closely.

client.name: Qortuba Auto Imports
client.profile: Spare parts importer, client for 4 years. Fast-moving inventory, reliable LC history. Today's request doesn't fit the man — or the business.

request: "I want to switch our LC line to 360-day usance, KD 700,000. Cash flow management, you understand — everyone's extending tenors these days. The parts business is the same as ever."

figures.label: Inventory turnover
figures.value: Parts sell in ~60 days (unchanged for years)

figures.label: New on balance sheet
figures.value: Land plot, KD 800,000, purchased 2 months ago — paid in cash

ratios.label: Cash conversion cycle
ratios.hint: Parts to cash in just over three months — among the fastest cycles on your desk.

ratios.label: Requested usance vs cycle
ratios.hint: He'd hold collected cash for ~9 months before paying the LC. That is not cash flow management; that is a money source.

ratios.label: Cash position
ratios.value: Down KD 750,000 since the land purchase
ratios.hint: The land emptied the company's cash. The 360-day usance would quietly refill it — with the bank's trade line.

decisions.prompt: A 60-day business asking for 360-day usance, two months after a cash land purchase. Read the file.

options.label: The land purchase drained the company's cash, and the 360-day usance is designed to refinance it through the trade line — diversion by tenor
options.feedback: The timeline tells it: cash bought land, and now supplier credit (bank-accepted) would replace the cash. The trade facility would silently carry a real estate position.

options.label: Sensible treasury management — longer payment terms are free money
options.feedback: Free money for what? The parts repay themselves in 95 days. The other 265 days of float exist to fund something that is not parts — and the balance sheet shows you what.

options.label: Industry-wide tenor extension — suppliers are simply offering more
options.feedback: Suppliers offer what importers ask for. The question is never what tenor is available, but what tenor the underlying trade cycle justifies. Here: 95 days, same as always.

options.label: Nothing notable — tenor preferences vary
options.feedback: A 4x mismatch between usance and cycle, synchronised with a cash-draining land purchase, is about as notable as trade finance red flags get.

decisions.prompt: Jassim is a good client who made an unfunded property move. Respond like a banker.

options.label: Usance at 90–120 days matching the cycle; separately, offer to discuss a properly secured term loan against the land if he needs liquidity
options.feedback: Both needs met, each in its own instrument: the trade line stays self-liquidating, and the land — if he wants cash against it — gets a term loan with a mortgage, priced and secured for what it is.

options.label: Approve the 360 days — the LC history is spotless
options.feedback: The spotless history was built on matched tenors. You've now embedded a 9-month unsecured property exposure inside a trade line, invisible to every report that matters.

options.label: Compromise at 180 days
options.feedback: Half the diversion is still diversion — 85 days of float with no trade purpose, just smaller. Splitting the difference isn't structure.

options.label: Decline the renewal entirely — the request reveals intent
options.feedback: He has a real, healthy parts business that genuinely earns its 90-120 day line. Punishing the core trade for a clumsy side-move loses a good client over a conversation you haven't had yet.

decisions.prompt: Terms for the renewed (90–120 day) trade line?

options.label: Existing margin + PG, plus a usage condition: usance tenor capped at the documented trade cycle, reviewed annually
options.feedback: The cap turns this year's lesson into permanent structure — tenor follows the cycle by rule, not by negotiation, every renewal from now on.

options.label: Existing security unchanged
options.feedback: The line was and remains adequately secured — though after this request, writing the tenor-cycle cap into the terms would cost nothing and prevent the sequel.

options.label: Take a mortgage over the new land as additional comfort on the trade line
options.feedback: Cross-collateralising the trade line with the land blesses the exact entanglement you just refused — now the LC line and the property really are one exposure.

options.label: Raise the cash margin to 50% as a penalty for the attempt
options.feedback: Punitive margining for a request you declined teaches resentment, not structure. The answer was no; the relationship continues.

learn: When requested tenor detaches from the trade cycle, the float is funding something else — find it on the balance sheet. Finance each need in its own instrument: trade at cycle tenor, property on a secured term loan.

client.name: Hawally Hypermarket Group
client.profile: Successful three-branch grocery retailer, client for 6 years. Wants to open three more branches. A junior analyst pre-reviewed the file and recommended declining for 'severe liquidity weakness'.

request: "Three new branches, KD 2,100,000 of fit-out and equipment. Term loan, please. Also — your analyst sent us a worrying note about our 'liquidity problem'. We don't have a liquidity problem. Do we?"

ratios.label: Current ratio
ratios.hint: Frightening out of context. In context: see the working capital line below.

ratios.label: Working capital cycle
ratios.hint: NEGATIVE cycle: customers pay cash today; suppliers wait 92 days. Suppliers fund the whole operation and 54 days of float besides. For grocery retail this is strength, not distress.

ratios.label: DSCR on requested TL (6 yrs)
ratios.hint: Comfortable on existing cash flow, before the new branches contribute anything.

decisions.prompt: First — was the analyst right? What does a 0.6x current ratio mean HERE?

options.label: Wrong call: negative working capital is the grocery model working — cash sales, supplier terms, no receivables. The 0.6x is structural strength misread as weakness
options.feedback: Benchmarks have sectors. A contractor at 0.6x is drowning; a cash-sales grocer at 0.6x is being financed by its suppliers — the strongest working capital position in commerce. Read the model, then the ratio.

options.label: The analyst is right — sub-1.0x current ratio is a hard stop regardless of industry
options.feedback: Ratio fundamentalism. Applied to retail, the 'hard stop' would decline every successful supermarket chain on earth — all of which run negative working capital on purpose.

options.label: Genuine concern: if sales dip, those 92-day payables come due against a thin cushion
options.feedback: The one real vulnerability of the model — it runs on velocity, and a sharp sales drop does bite. Worth a covenant; not a reason to misdiagnose a healthy structure as a sick one.

options.label: The ratios conflict, so the financials are probably unreliable
options.feedback: Nothing conflicts — every number tells the same coherent retail story. The inconsistency was in the analysis, not the accounts.

decisions.prompt: Now the expansion. Structure it.

options.label: Term Loan KD 2,100,000 over 6 years for the fit-out — no working capital facility needed; the model self-funds operations
options.feedback: Clean: term money for the fixed assets at 1.7x DSCR, and the recognition that this client needs no STRL is itself correct analysis — new branches generate cash from day one of trading.

options.label: TL 2,100,000 + STRL KD 1,000,000 'to be safe' on the expansion
options.feedback: A working capital line for a negative-working-capital business is a limit in search of a purpose — and idle limits find purposes. Lend what the model needs, which here is fit-out only.

options.label: Decline per the analyst's liquidity memo
options.feedback: Declining a 14.5M-revenue, 6-year client at 1.7x DSCR because a ratio was read without its sector — the competitor who understands retail will write this loan by Thursday.

options.label: TL KD 1,400,000 — fund two branches first, third on results
options.feedback: Sensible conservatism, defensible at committee — though with DSCR at 1.7x before any new-branch contribution, the staging arguably under-backs a proven operator's plan.

decisions.prompt: Security and conditions for the expansion loan?

options.label: Lien over fit-out & equipment + corporate guarantee + minimum-sales covenant per new branch
options.feedback: The covenant watches the model's one weak point — velocity. If a new branch underperforms, you know at the quarter, not at the default.

options.label: Lien over fit-out & equipment + PG
options.feedback: Adequate and proportionate — though for a velocity-dependent model, the sales covenant is the early-warning system worth one more paragraph in the agreement.

options.label: Require a 100% cash margin given the 'weak liquidity'
options.feedback: Still pricing the misdiagnosis. Demanding blocked cash from a supplier-financed retailer repeats the analyst's error with money attached.

options.label: Mortgage over one of the existing branch premises
options.feedback: The branches are leased — there's likely nothing to mortgage. The pack's asset story points at equipment, not property.

facilitySummary: Term Loan KD 2.1M / 6 years (3 new branches)
learn: Ratios mean nothing without the business model: negative working capital is distress in contracting and excellence in cash retail. Benchmark within the sector — and covenant the model's actual weak point, not the textbook's.

client.name: Sulaibiya Steel Fabrication
client.profile: Aggressive operator who doubled the company in 18 months. Charismatic, persuasive, always in a hurry. Account conduct has developed cracks the growth story doesn't mention.

request: "Revenue has DOUBLED in eighteen months and the order book is overflowing. I need all limits up 50% — today, ideally. Banks that move slowly lose clients like me. Are you a bank that moves slowly?"

figures.label: Gross margin
figures.hint: He's buying the growth — winning orders on price.

figures.label: Account conduct
figures.value: 2 returned cheques in 4 months ('technical errors'); 3 excesses over OD limit, regularised late

ratios.label: Leverage (Debt / Equity)
ratios.hint: Past the line and climbing — the growth is debt all the way down.

ratios.label: Working capital absorption
ratios.value: Every dinar of profit + new debt is consumed by WIP and receivables
ratios.hint: Classic overtrading mechanics: the order book eats cash faster than it returns it.

ratios.label: Interest cover
ratios.hint: Margin erosion and debt growth compounding into the same number.

decisions.prompt: Strip away the charisma. What is this file?

options.label: Late-stage overtrading: debt-fueled growth at collapsing margins, with the returned cheques as the first public symptom of cash exhaustion
options.feedback: All four gauges agree — leverage, margins, payables, conduct. The returned cheques are the part other creditors can see; the balance sheet explains why they happened.

options.label: A growth company with timing issues — the order book will cure the cash flow
options.feedback: The order book is the cause, not the cure: at 8% margins, every new order consumes more cash in WIP than it returns in profit. More orders make it worse. That's the overtrading trap in one sentence.

options.label: Two returned cheques in four months — exit the relationship now
options.feedback: The cheques are a symptom demanding investigation and de-risking, not a panic trigger. A managed tightening can still save this client — and the bank's money. Abandonment saves neither.

options.label: Healthy expansion with normal growing pains
options.feedback: Margins down 43%, leverage past 2x, suppliers waiting 95 days, cheques bouncing. If these are growing pains, the next stage of growth is insolvency.

decisions.prompt: He's across the desk, waiting for his 50%. Decide.

options.label: No increases. Hold limits, require a capital injection plan and monthly management accounts, move all lines to secured basis with assignment of contract proceeds
options.feedback: The intervention that can still work: the company needs equity and pricing discipline, not more debt — and the monthly numbers will show within a quarter whether Mishal heard you.

options.label: Approve the 50% — back the order book, momentum is real
options.feedback: You just leveraged an overtrader past the point of return with the bank's money. When the cash runs out — and at 8% margins it will — the bank is the largest creditor at the table.

options.label: Offer +20% as a compromise to keep him engaged
options.feedback: Smaller fuel on the same fire. Any new debt deepens the mechanics; the compromise buys his goodwill with the bank's principal.

options.label: Freeze all utilisation and demand early repayment
options.feedback: An instant freeze mid-WIP strands live projects, triggers cross-defaults, and converts a salvageable overtrader into a certain loss. De-risking is a staircase, not a trapdoor.

decisions.prompt: Last point — the two returned cheques. Mishal calls them 'technical errors'. What do they mean to you?

options.label: Near-conclusive cash exhaustion: companies pay cheques before almost anything — bounced ones mean the buffer is gone. 'Technical error', twice, is a story
options.feedback: Returned cheques are the canary of corporate distress in this market — visible to every bank, every supplier, and the credit bureau. Two in four months means the cash is gone and the juggling has begun.

options.label: Probably genuine errors — modern payment systems misfire sometimes
options.feedback: Once, perhaps. Twice, during a cash squeeze visible across the entire balance sheet, while suppliers wait 95 days? The kindest reading is still distress.

options.label: Relevant only if a cheque to our bank bounces
options.feedback: His cheques to anyone are signals about the same cash pool that repays us. Conduct intelligence doesn't respect whose name is on the payee line.

options.label: A pricing opportunity — raise his rates to match the risk
options.feedback: Repricing a deteriorating exposure without de-risking it earns an extra half-percent on money you're about to lose. Risk action first; pricing follows structure.

facilitySummary: Limits held; capital plan required (Sulaibiya Steel)

plantedError.prompt: While re-papering the lines onto a secured basis, documentation runs its checks. What surfaces?

options.label: The board resolution on file names a general manager who left the company a year ago as sole authorised signatory
options.feedback: Correct — every document signed since his departure is potentially voidable. A current board resolution and updated signatory cards are needed before any re-papering. Authorisations age; check them at every major event.

options.label: The file uses the company's old logo on some documents
options.feedback: Branding has no legal weight — signatures and authorisations do.

options.label: Nothing — proceed with re-papering
options.feedback: The signatory authorisation is a year out of date and names someone who left. That invalidates the chain — fix it first.

learn: Overtrading endgame: doubling revenue at collapsing margins, financed by suppliers and debt, until the cheques start bouncing. The cure is equity and discipline — never more debt. And returned cheques are never 'technical errors' twice.
